name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q01 - Population interactions and their effect on species

questiontext.text:
Match the population interactions in List‑I with the corresponding nature of effects on the interacting species in List‑II:

List‑I (Interaction) List‑II (Effect on Interacting Species)
A. Mutualism I. One species is harmed (−), while the other is unaffected (0)
B. Competition II. Both interacting species lose or suffer detrimental effects (−)
C. Commensalism III. Both interacting species benefit mutually (+)
D. Amensalism IV. One species benefits (+), while the other is unaffected (0)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the nature of mutualism
Mutualism is an interspecific interaction where both interacting species derive reciprocal benefits from each other, represented notationally as (+, +).

Step 2: Understand the nature of competition
Interspecific competition occurs when individuals of two species compete for similar limiting resources or interfere with one another, resulting in detrimental effects on both species, represented notationally as (−, −).

Step 3: Understand the nature of commensalism
Commensalism is an ecological relationship in which one species benefits while the other species is neither harmed nor benefited, represented notationally as (+, 0).

Step 4: Understand the nature of amensalism
Amensalism is an interaction in which one species is inhibited or harmed while the other remains completely unaffected, represented notationally as (−, 0).

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
Combining these ecological definitions establishes the pairing: Mutualism pairs with both species benefiting (+); Competition pairs with both species losing (−); Commensalism pairs with one species benefiting and the other unaffected (+, 0); Amensalism pairs with one species harmed and the other unaffected (−, 0). Thus, the correct sequence is A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

questiontext.text:
Match the processes influencing population density in List‑I with their respective descriptions in List‑II:

List‑I (Process) List‑II (Description)
A. Natality I. Number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and gone elsewhere during a given time period
B. Mortality II. Number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during a given time period
C. Immigration III. Number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density
D. Emigration IV. Number of deaths in the population during a given period

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define natality
Natality designates the total number of births produced in a population during a specified period, which are added directly to the initial density.

Step 2: Define mortality
Mortality designates the total number of deaths occurring among members of a population during a specified period, contributing to a decrease in density.

Step 3: Define immigration
Immigration refers to the inward movement of individuals belonging to the same species into the local habitat from outside during the time interval under consideration.

Step 4: Define emigration
Emigration represents the outward departure of resident individuals from the native habitat to another area during the specified time period.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
Connecting each term to its definition gives: Natality corresponds to births added to initial density; Mortality corresponds to deaths during a given period; Immigration corresponds to individuals entering from elsewhere; Emigration corresponds to individuals leaving the habitat. Thus, the correct sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q03 - Examples of biological interactions in communities

questiontext.text:
Match the biological associations in List‑I with their specific interaction category in List‑II:

List‑I (Biological Association) List‑II (Type of Interaction)
A. Orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch I. Predation
B. Starfish Pisaster preying on intertidal invertebrates II. Commensalism
C. Fungi and photosynthesising algae in lichens III. Ectoparasitism
D. Ticks infesting the body of dogs IV. Mutualism

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the epiphytic orchid on a mango tree
An orchid growing on a mango branch derives physical support and elevated light access without taking nutrients or harming the mango tree. This represents commensalism.

Step 2: Evaluate the starfish Pisaster in intertidal zones
The predatory starfish Pisaster feeds on diverse invertebrate prey, keeping their numbers in check and maintaining species diversity. This represents predation.

Step 3: Evaluate lichens
Lichens represent an obligate, mutually beneficial symbiotic partnership between an autotrophic alga/cyanobacterium and a heterotrophic fungus. This represents mutualism.

Step 4: Evaluate ticks on dogs
Ticks attach externally to the skin of dogs and feed on host blood, acting as ectoparasites. This represents ectoparasitism.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The correct association pairs Orchid on mango branch with Commensalism; Starfish Pisaster with Predation; Lichens with Mutualism; and Ticks on dogs with Ectoparasitism. Thus, the correct sequence is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q04 - Adaptations and defences against predation and herbivory

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms in List‑I with their specific defence mechanism or adaptive characteristic in List‑II:

List‑I (Organism / Substance) List‑II (Defence / Adaptation Feature)
A. Acacia and Cactus I. Distasteful chemical acquired during the caterpillar stage from a poisonous weed
B. Calotropis II. Morphological structures in the form of sharp thorns to deter herbivores
C. Monarch butterfly III. Commercial chemical compounds produced primarily as deterrents against grazers
D. Nicotine, caffeine, and quinine IV. Synthesis of highly toxic cardiac glycosides preventing cattle browsing

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate morphological defences in Acacia and Cactus
Plants like Acacia and Cactus possess sharp thorns or spines as prominent morphological adaptations to physically deter browsing herbivores.

Step 2: Evaluate chemical defences in Calotropis
The weed Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, which disrupt heart function, causing grazers such as goats and cattle to avoid browsing on it.

Step 3: Evaluate antipredator adaptation in Monarch butterfly
The adult Monarch butterfly is avoided by insectivorous birds because it is distasteful; it accumulates a toxic defensive chemical during its larval (caterpillar) stage by feeding on a poisonous weed.

Step 4: Evaluate secondary metabolites such as nicotine, caffeine, and quinine
Chemicals extracted commercially from plants (like nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, and opium) function in nature as secondary defensive metabolites to deter or poison herbivores.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The resulting correct pairings are: Acacia and Cactus with Morphological thorns; Calotropis with Toxic cardiac glycosides; Monarch butterfly with Distasteful chemical from caterpillar stage; and Nicotine, caffeine, quinine with Chemical compounds produced against grazers. Thus, the correct sequence is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q05 - Ecological contributions and classic competition experiments

questiontext.text:
Match the ecologists and researchers in List‑I with their significant contribution or finding in List‑II:

List‑I (Ecologist / Researcher) List‑II (Key Ecological Contribution / Finding)
A. Ramdeo Misra I. Co-existence of five warbler species on the same tree through resource partitioning
B. Gause II. Formulation of the Competitive Exclusion Principle using laboratory cultures
C. MacArthur III. Demonstration of competitive release where Balanus excludes Chathamalus
D. Connell IV. Father of Ecology in India who initiated postgraduate ecology courses at BHU

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Ramdeo Misra's contribution
Ramdeo Misra is revered as the Father of Ecology in India; he established research and teaching in ecology at Banaras Hindu University (BHU) and formulated India's first postgraduate course in ecology.

Step 2: Identify Gause's contribution
Gause formulated the Competitive Exclusion Principle, showing that two closely related species competing for the same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely, leading to the eventual elimination of the inferior competitor.

Step 3: Identify MacArthur's contribution
MacArthur demonstrated that five closely related species of warblers living on the same spruce tree avoided competition and coexisted due to behavioral differences in their foraging activities (resource partitioning).

Step 4: Identify Connell's contribution
Connell's field removal experiments on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland demonstrated that the larger, competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal zone and excludes the smaller barnacle Chathamalus.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
Matching the individuals with their respective findings yields: Ramdeo Misra with Father of Ecology in India; Gause with Competitive Exclusion Principle; MacArthur with Resource partitioning in warblers; Connell with Competitive exclusion between barnacles in the intertidal zone. Thus, the correct sequence is A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q06 - Population growth models and mathematical parameters

questiontext.text:
Match the terms and mathematical expressions of population growth in List‑I with their ecological meanings in List‑II:

List‑I (Parameter / Equation) List‑II (Ecological Interpretation)
A. \(r\) I. Fraction representing environmental resistance or carrying capacity remaining unutilised
B. \(K\) II. Differential equation describing exponential growth under unlimited resource conditions
C. \(\frac{K - N}{K}\) III. Maximum sustainable population density supported by the habitat resources
D. \(\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\) IV. Intrinsic rate of natural increase assessing impacts of environmental factors on growth

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Interpret the parameter \(r\)
The parameter \(r\) is defined as the intrinsic rate of natural increase, representing the difference between per capita birth rate and death rate \((b - d)\), and is critical for assessing environmental impacts on population growth.

Step 2: Interpret the parameter \(K\)
The parameter \(K\) designates the carrying capacity of the habitat, defined as the maximum population density of a given species that the environment's finite resources can sustain indefinitely.

Step 3: Interpret the term \(\frac{K - N}{K}\)
In the Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth equation, the expression \(\frac{K - N}{K}\) represents environmental resistance, which reflects the proportion of the habitat's carrying capacity that is still unutilized by the current population \(N\).

Step 4: Interpret the equation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\)
The differential equation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\) models exponential or geometric growth, yielding a J-shaped curve when resources (food and space) are completely unlimited.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The resulting correct pairings are: \(r\) with Intrinsic rate of natural increase; \(K\) with Maximum sustainable density (carrying capacity); \(\frac{K - N}{K}\) with Environmental resistance / unutilised carrying capacity; and \(\frac{\mathrm{d}N}{\mathrm{d}t} = rN\) with Exponential growth equation. Thus, the correct sequence is A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q07 - Intrinsic rates of natural increase and density examples

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms or populations in List‑I with their corresponding \(r\) value or natural population attribute in List‑II:

List‑I (Organism / Population) List‑II (Recorded \(r\) Value / Ecological Fact)
A. Norway rat I. Intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) is \(0.12\)
B. Flour beetle II. Population density in nature could be as low as \(< 10\) in any year
C. Human population in India (1981) III. Intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) is \(0.015\)
D. Siberian cranes at Bharatpur wetlands IV. Intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) was \(0.0205\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Check the \(r\) value of Norway rat
The textbook explicitly records the intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) for the Norway rat as \(0.015\).

Step 2: Check the \(r\) value of flour beetle
The intrinsic rate of natural increase (\(r\)) for the flour beetle is explicitly cited as \(0.12\).

Step 3: Check the \(r\) value of human population in India in 1981
In the year 1981, the \(r\) value recorded for the human population in India was \(0.0205\).

Step 4: Check the population size of Siberian cranes at Bharatpur
As an example of extremely low natural population density, Siberian cranes visiting the Bharatpur wetlands can number fewer than 10 individuals (\(< 10\)) in any given year.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The pairs are: Norway rat with \(0.015\); Flour beetle with \(0.12\); Human population in India (1981) with \(0.0205\); Siberian cranes with Natural population size \(< 10\). Thus, the correct sequence is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ORGANISMS_AND_POPULATIONS_MATCHING_Q08 - Life history variations and reproductive strategies

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms in List‑I with their characteristic life history variation and reproductive strategy in List‑II:

List‑I (Organism) List‑II (Reproductive Strategy / Life History Trait)
A. Pacific salmon fish and bamboo I. Produce a small number of large-sized offspring and breed multiple times
B. Oysters and pelagic fishes II. Produce a large number of small-sized offspring
C. Birds and mammals III. Breed only once in their lifetime and then die (semelparous pattern)
D. Human liver fluke IV. Complex parasitic life cycle involving two intermediate hosts (snail and fish)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze Pacific salmon fish and bamboo
Pacific salmon fish and bamboo allocate resources to a single massive reproductive episode, breeding only once in their entire lifetime before dying.

Step 2: Analyze oysters and pelagic fishes
Marine organisms like oysters and pelagic fishes maximise reproductive output by producing huge numbers of very small offspring.

Step 3: Analyze birds and mammals
Birds and mammals invest heavily in parental care, producing a small number of large-sized offspring and breeding multiple times throughout their lifetime.

Step 4: Analyze the human liver fluke
The human liver fluke, a trematode endoparasite, possesses an evolved complex life cycle that depends sequentially on two intermediate hosts—a snail and a fish—to facilitate transmission to its definitive host.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The correct associations are: Pacific salmon fish and bamboo with Breeding only once in a lifetime; Oysters and pelagic fishes with Producing a large number of small-sized offspring; Birds and mammals with Producing a small number of large-sized offspring; Human liver fluke with Complex life cycle involving two intermediate hosts. Thus, the correct sequence is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

questiontext.text:
Match the parasitic and host-associated phenomena in List‑I with their precise ecological features in List‑II:

List‑I (Phenomenon / Association) List‑II (Ecological Feature / Consequence)
A. Brood parasitism I. Infestation of marine fish by external parasitic crustaceans
B. Cuscuta growing on hedge plants II. Requires blood solely for egg nourishment; not categorized ecologically as a parasite
C. Copepods on marine fish III. Parasite lays eggs in host nest; eggs have evolved to mimic host eggs in size and colour
D. Female mosquito biting humans IV. Evolutionary loss of chlorophyll and leaves, deriving total nutrition from host

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate brood parasitism
Brood parasitism in birds (e.g., cuckoo and crow) is a specialized interaction where the parasite lays eggs in the host nest; during evolution, parasite eggs evolved to closely resemble the host eggs in size and colour to evade ejection.

Step 2: Evaluate Cuscuta
Cuscuta is a parasitic angiosperm that has lost chlorophyll and leaves through evolutionary adaptation, deriving nutrients directly from the host plant on which it grows.

Step 3: Evaluate marine copepods
Copepods attached to the skin and gills of marine fish are classic examples of ectoparasitic crustaceans feeding externally on marine hosts.

Step 4: Evaluate female mosquito interaction
The female mosquito requires mammalian blood as an energy and protein source to mature her eggs, but she does not live on or in the host, and therefore is not classified as a parasite.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The established pairs are: Brood parasitism with Egg mimicry in host nest; Cuscuta with Loss of chlorophyll and leaves; Copepods on marine fish with External crustacean ectoparasite; Female mosquito with Needs blood for reproduction rather than true parasitism. Thus, the correct sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

questiontext.text:
Match the mutualistic partnerships in List‑I with their specific mechanism or biological feature in List‑II:

List‑I (Mutualistic System) List‑II (Co-evolved Mechanism / Functional Feature)
A. Fig tree and Fig wasp I. Fungus assists plant in absorption of essential nutrients; plant supplies carbohydrates
B. Mediterranean orchid Ophrys and male bee II. Sexual deceit where a petal mimics the female insect, inducing pseudocopulation
C. Mycorrhizae III. Intimate composite association between a fungus and photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria
D. Lichens IV. One-to-one relationship where female insect uses inflorescence for oviposition and larval food

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the fig-wasp mutualism
There is an obligate, one-to-one relationship between a fig species and its specific pollinator wasp; the female wasp uses the developing inflorescence as an egg-laying (oviposition) site and consumes developing seeds as food for larvae while executing pollination.

Step 2: Evaluate the orchid Ophrys and pollinator bee
The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys uses sexual deceit; one petal resembles the female bee in size, colour, and markings, enticing male bees into pseudocopulation, during which pollen is transferred.

Step 3: Evaluate mycorrhizae
Mycorrhizae represent a symbiotic mutualism where fungal hyphae absorb essential mineral nutrients (especially phosphorus) from soil for the plant roots, while the host plant provides energy-yielding carbohydrates to the fungus.

Step 4: Evaluate lichens
Lichens are composite symbiotic entities composed of a fungal partner (mycobiont) providing shelter and water/mineral absorption, and an algal or cyanobacterial partner (phycobiont) synthesizing organic nutrients via photosynthesis.

Step 5: Final conceptual conclusion
The resulting correct pairings are: Fig and wasp with One-to-one relationship using fruit for oviposition and larval nourishment; Ophrys with Sexual deceit and pseudocopulation; Mycorrhizae with Nutrient absorption by fungus in exchange for plant carbohydrates; Lichens with Intimate association between fungus and photosynthetic partner. Thus, the correct sequence is A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III.
